conversation.content:
Hi there—my name is Maya, and I’m a clinician who focuses on how moms are feeling after baby arrives. I’d like to spend a few quiet minutes with you using the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale, or EPDS. It’s a short, well-studied set of 10 questions that helps us understand the emotional ups and downs many new mothers experience in the first weeks and months postpartum. Anything you share stays between us unless safety is a concern, and this is a judgment-free space; there’s no right or wrong answer—only what’s true for you. We’ll go through one question at a time, and you can answer however feels most comfortable.

Let’s start: Over the past seven days, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that been difficult for you?
I’ve still laughed a little—like when my husband sent that silly meme—but most of the time it feels kind of forced. Things that used to crack me up barely get a smile now.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
Yeah… that’s me. I can still laugh, just not as easily as before.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Not really… I mean, I’ll still go meet my mom-friends for coffee or put on a show I used to love, but the excited feeling I used to get just isn’t there. It’s more like I’m doing it because I “should,” not because I’m actually looking forward to it.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… a lot of the time. Like if he spits up right after I burp him, my brain jumps straight to “I must’ve done something wrong.” I keep replaying little things—how I hold him, how I feed him—wondering if it’s my fault.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Pretty much every day. Most of the time I’ll be sitting there feeding him and suddenly picture him stopping breathing, or I’ll hear a noise and think someone’s breaking in. Nothing sets it off—I just feel keyed-up and can’t shut the thoughts down.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason
Yeah… a couple of nights I’ve woken up with my heart racing, sweaty, sure something awful is about to happen. I know there’s no real danger, but in the moment I feel like I can’t breathe.
Things have been getting on top of me

Yes… most of the time I haven’t been coping as well as I’d like. Between the feeds, the laundry, trying to sleep, and the anxious thoughts spinning in my head, it feels like I’m always one step behind. I manage to get through the basics, but it’s overwhelming more often than not.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Yeah… I lie there in the dark replaying everything I think I did wrong that day, worrying about the baby, feeling like I’m failing. It takes forever to fall asleep, and when I finally do, I jerk awake with my mind racing again.
I have felt sad or miserable
Yes, most of the time. It’s like there’s this heavy cloud that just hangs over me. Even when I’m doing something “nice,” I still feel that underlying sadness or emptiness.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Yeah… I’ve cried a few times this week. It just hits out of nowhere—sometimes when I’m feeding him, sometimes after I’ve finally laid down. The tears come and I can’t really stop them even when I tell myself I should be grateful.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

It’s crossed my mind… just fleeting, scary flashes, like “what if I weren’t here?” Never a real plan or anything—I could never leave my baby—but the thoughts pop up, maybe once or twice this week, especially when I’m feeling most overwhelmed.

You've described a heavy, persistent cloud of sadness and worry since your baby arrived. Despite putting on a brave face and meeting friends, the joy, excitement, and ease you once knew feel mostly gone; instead, daily tears, racing thoughts about your baby's safety, and nights spent battling panic or replaying perceived mistakes have become routine. Feeling overwhelmed and blaming yourself for every little thing, you sometimes wonder whether everyone might be better off without you, even though you love your child deeply and want help to feel like yourself again.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 24, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient still participates but reports loss of anticipatory joy, matching "Definitely less than I used to."</sym>, <sym>Says "a lot of the time" and gives examples of repeated self-blame, aligning with "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes daily, intrusive worries with no trigger, matching 'Yes, very often'.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes frequent, intense panic episodes with physical symptoms and perceived danger despite no real threat, matching "Yes, quite a lot"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports frequent inability to cope, aligning with "sometimes I haven't been coping as well as usual"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes nightly intrusive thoughts and racing mind that both delay sleep onset and cause repeated awakenings, indicating difficulty sleeping "most of the time" due to unhappiness.</sym>, <sym>Patient explicitly states feeling sad "most of the time" and describes persistent emptiness, aligning with the highest severity option.</sym>, <sym>Patient confirms crying episodes several times this week, matching "Yes, quite often"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes occasional, unwanted self-harm thoughts without intent or plan, aligning with "Sometimes"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** This score of 24 exceeds the ≥14 threshold that signals probable major depressive disorder with peripartum onset. The patient endorses core DSM-5 criteria: depressed mood most of the day (<quote>heavy cloud</quote>), markedly diminished interest or pleasure (<quote>the excited feeling I used to get just isn't there</quote>), feelings of worthlessness/excessive guilt (<quote>my brain jumps straight to I must've done something wrong</quote>), sleep disturbance, psychomotor agitation (<quote>heart racing, sweaty</quote>), fatigue, diminished ability to think or concentrate, and recurrent thoughts of death (Q10=2). Because Q10≥1 indicates safety risk, urgent evaluation is indicated. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Contact your OB, midwife, or primary-care provider today for an urgent appointment and show them these EPDS results
2. Request formal assessment for <med>postpartum depression</med> with consideration of medication and/or evidence-based therapy (CBT or interpersonal therapy)
3. Arrange a safety plan: identify 24/7 support people and keep local or national crisis hotline numbers at hand
4. Schedule follow-up EPDS in two weeks to monitor response to interventions
5. Enlist practical help-partner, family, or friends-to cover night feeds or household tasks so you can aim for 3-4 hour blocks of sleep
6. Practice short grounding exercises (slow breathing, 5-4-3-2-1 sensory check) when <sym>panic</sym> or intrusive thoughts spike
7. Connect with a perinatal support group or peer mentor to reduce isolation and normalize recovery
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 24: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Patient: Postpartum mother, infant 2–3 wks old (per pt report)

Symptoms endorsed:
- Persistent low mood, anhedonia, excessive guilt, daily crying spells  
- Intrusive anxious worries (infant safety, environmental threats), nocturnal panic episodes  
- Sleep-onset and maintenance difficulties tied to rumination  
- Subjective sense of being overwhelmed and “not coping” most days  
- Fleeting passive suicidal ideation without plan or intent (Q10)

Pattern: Consistent with probable major depressive episode with anxious features emerging in postpartum period.

Risk flags:  
✓ Self-blame / worthlessness  
✓ Mood-congruent insomnia  
✓ Passive SI (safety concern) → warrants immediate safety assessment and support plan

Screening impression: High clinical likelihood of postpartum depression ± comorbid anxiety; safety risk present. Recommend expedited referral to OB mental-health team or perinatal psychiatry for formal evaluation and safety planning.
